concepts.topicTitle: What development promises: different people, different goals
concepts.label: Different People, Different Developmental Goals
concepts.cardText: Different persons seek different things: what is most important for them, given their aspirations. Landless rural labourers want more days of work and better wages; prosperous farmers from Punjab want higher support prices for their crops. Goals can even conflict: industrialists may want more dams for electricity, but dams may submerge land and displace people such as tribals. So different persons can have different developmental goals, and what is development for one may not be development for another; it may even be destructive.

concepts.topicTitle: What development promises: different people, different goals
concepts.label: Income and Other Goals
concepts.cardText: Most people want more income: regular work, better wages and decent prices for their crops. But people also seek equal treatment, freedom, security and respect of others, and resent discrimination. In some cases these matter more than income, because material goods are not all that you need to live. The quality of our life also depends on non-material things, and it is wrong to conclude that what cannot be measured is not important. So developmental goals are about better income and other important things in life.

concepts.topicTitle: What development promises: different people, different goals
concepts.label: National Development
concepts.cardText: If individuals seek different goals, their notions of national development will also differ, and may even conflict. National development means thinking about questions such as: can all ideas be considered equally important; if there are conflicts, how does one decide; what would be a fair and just path for all; is there a better way of doing things; and would the idea benefit a large number of people or only a small group?

concepts.topicTitle: How to compare different countries or states?
concepts.label: Per Capita Income and the World Bank
concepts.cardText: For comparing countries, income is considered one of the most important attributes, since more income is understood to mean more of all things people need. Total income is not useful for comparison because countries have different populations, so we compare average income: the total income of the country divided by its total population, also called per capita income. The World Bank's World Development Reports use this to classify countries: in 2024, countries with per capita income of US$ 66,500 and above are high income, and those with about US$ 2,300 or less are low-income. India, at about US$ 11,000, is a low middle income country.

concepts.topicTitle: How to compare different countries or states?
concepts.label: Averages Hide Disparities
concepts.cardText: Averages are useful for comparison, but they also hide disparities. Countries A and B can have the same average income: in A, citizens are neither very rich nor extremely poor; in B, most citizens are poor and one person is extremely rich. Most of us would prefer to live in A because it has a more equitable distribution. So while average income is useful for comparison, it does not tell us how income is distributed among people.

concepts.label: Income and Other Criteria: Kerala and Haryana
concepts.cardText: Haryana has the highest per capita income of Haryana, Kerala and Bihar, and Bihar the lowest. By income alone, Haryana would be the most developed. But in Kerala, 6 of every 1000 children die before age one, against 28 in Haryana, nearly three times more. About one-third of children aged 15-17 in Bihar are not attending school. So, besides average income, we must consider other attributes like health and education. The Infant Mortality Rate is the number of children who die before age one per 1000 live births.

concepts.label: Public Facilities
concepts.cardText: Money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services you need to live well. It cannot normally buy a pollution-free environment or ensure unadulterated medicines, or protect you from infectious diseases unless the whole community takes preventive steps. For many important things, the best and cheapest way is to provide them collectively, like security for a whole locality or schools for all children. Kerala has a low Infant Mortality Rate because it has adequate basic health and educational facilities; where the Public Distribution System functions well, health and nutrition are likely to be better.

concepts.label: Human Development Report
concepts.cardText: Income is important but an inadequate measure of development, so health and education indicators are now widely used along with income. The Human Development Report published by UNDP compares countries based on the educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income. Sri Lanka, a small neighbour, is much ahead of India in every respect, and Nepal and Bangladesh have lower per capita income than India but better life expectancy. By prefixing 'Human' to development, the report makes clear that what matters is what happens to the citizens of a country.

concepts.label: Sustainability of Development
concepts.cardText: We want development to go up, or at least be maintained for future generations, but scientists warn that the present type and levels of development are not sustainable. Groundwater is a renewable resource, replenished by rain, but it can be overused: nearly one-third of India is overusing its groundwater, especially in Punjab and Western U.P. Non-renewable resources, like crude oil, have a fixed stock and will be exhausted; world reserves would last only about 50 years more. Environmental degradation does not respect national or state boundaries.
